title: The man who saw the 1859 flare doubted it caused the storm.
description:
The man who saw the 1859 flare doubted it caused the storm. Richard Carrington wrote that one swallow does not make a summer.

Two British astronomers who saw the flare independently, just before noon on 1 September.

The aurora was reported close to the equator. Sightings came from Cuba, Hawaii and Colombia, far further south than usual.

Telegraph equipment shocked operators and threw sparks. NOAA also records small fires, and messages arriving that no one had sent.

Two operators between Boston and Portland worked with their batteries disconnected, powered by the sky alone.

He saw it first and doubted it most.

Sources:
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carrington_Event - Wikipedia; established that Richard Carrington and Richard Hodgson independently saw the flare just before noon on 1 September 1859, that Carrington himself wrote that one swallow does not make a summer about linking it to the storm, that aurora was reported near the equator, that telegraph pylons threw sparks, and that two operators between Boston and Portland worked for about two hours on auroral current with their batteries disconnected. Also the March 1989 Quebec outage and a 2013 Lloyd's estimate of $600 billion to $2.6 trillion, described there as speculative.
- https://www.noaa.gov/heritage/stories/five-historically-huge-solar-events - NOAA; established the date of 1 September 1859, that Carrington and Hodgson saw it independently, that the aurora was seen further south than ever recorded, that telegraph operators were shocked and small fires started, and that some machines sent messages without being plugged in.
